answer:
I checked the Hormozi vault. Here is his answer.

**Verdict:** Raise your prices first. Don't add clients at your current rate. At $35k a month he'd see charging more as one of your biggest levers. More clients at the same price would just fill up a 4-person team.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing on agencies specifically. He did say this to a service business doing about $1.25M a year, and to service businesses in general.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Price is the lever at your size.** He calls it big for owners under roughly $3–5M: "some of the biggest levers that exist in the business is simply charging more because people actually believe you can deliver the service now." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s))
- **A higher price can raise your close rate.** It raises "the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise" (@ 7:00). It also brings more committed and less demanding clients. That matters a lot in an agency.
- **Find your constraint first.** His first question is "is this a supply constraint business or a demand constraint business" (@ 3:47). A 4-person team usually runs out of people before it runs out of leads. Adding clients then makes that problem worse, and his rule for that case is "when you have demand, cut supply" ([[yt-uWdIgftpvBI]] @ 5:28, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=328s)).
- **Charge more by moving up-market.** "solve rich people problems they pay better" ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:38:38, [link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5918s)). At one PR company he backs, he cut the client list down to the 15% who bought the top package and stayed, then raised prices 10x.

**How to test it:** If you close more than 80% of the people you pitch, he'd say you're underpriced. Before raising, work out the close rate you need to break even at the new price. Then raise prices on new pitches first.

**What would change his answer:** Leads are the problem, not capacity. If your team has spare hours and not enough leads coming in, the constraint is demand. His fix for that is more and better marketing, not just a higher price.

**Verdict:** He'd most likely put the money into ads, not a salesperson, but only once you know that customers are what's holding you back. His first question is always "what's the constraint?" A salesperson fixes a closing problem. Most local cleaning businesses have a lead problem.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. He hasn't talked about cleaning businesses, but he has coached a duct-cleaning company and a roofing company through the same choice.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Start with supply or demand.** "the first problem I try to delineate is this is a supply constraint business or a demand constraint business." ([source @ 3:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=227s)) He also warns that owners often fix the wrong thing and make the real problem worse. If you can't staff the jobs you already have, spend the $10k on cleaners.
- **For demand, fix the cheap things before spending more.** He gave the duct-cleaning owner a ranked list: raise prices about 10%, build an ad landing page, fix the ads, and only then raise ad spend. "if we fix the landing page and we just improve the ads you have you might already double or triple your lead flow." ([@ 31:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1908s)) He also has you email past customers first. He calls that almost pure profit.
- **Then spend as much as the returns justify.** If ads pay back and you trust the tracking, spend "as many dollars as you possibly could" ([@ 11:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=681s)). If you can't tell what's paying back, he calls that "a data problem."
- **He adds salespeople only when the team is the bottleneck.** He told the roofing owner to recruit reps ("think about sales people as your new customers") when more salespeople were the limit and the owner already closed reliably by knocking doors ([@ 21:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1305s)). With a handful of reps, he said the owner could manage them himself.

**What would change his answer:** if you have more inbound leads than you can close, or you're already good at outbound selling like door-to-door, he'd tell you to put the money behind people.

My own note: $10k is roughly two to four months of a salesperson's pay before they've proven anything. The same money in ads lets you test small and scale up only what pays back.

**Verdict:** Cut it down. Hormozi says that after price, the number one reason people cancel is overwhelm, so adding more workouts and content will probably make cancellations worse. Find the one thing your members would fight to keep, make that excellent, and get each new member a win in their first 24 hours.

**Based on:** he said it. His 2026 retention talk addresses exactly this situation.

**Why he'd say it**
- Unused extras push people to cancel: "When you have five things that you pay for, but you only use one, you feel like you're only getting 20% of the value. If for the same price, you just offer that one thing, people feel like they're getting 100% of the value." ([How to Get Your Customers to Stay FOREVER @ 10:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=622s)) Adding content nobody uses means "all we did is we gave them more reason to cancel because they never used it." (@ 10:54)
- His test for what to keep is to ask members: "if I were to delete everything, what one thing would you fight for?" ([@ 11:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=686s)) Then focus on the top one or two answers.
- Members aren't using your program full-time, so give them a simple "start here" and weekly plan. Leave extra depth as optional for keen members, and "pin the fast win up front so new members hit that value ideally within the first 24 hours." ([@ 13:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=786s))
- Check this against your own data rather than guessing. Message everyone who cancels, tag the reason, and "for every 20 cancels or so, review the top one or two reasons, and then fix those." ([@ 6:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=395s)) Ask your longest-staying members why they stay, and do more of that.

**What he's done:** In his own Skool Games community, overwhelm was the top reason people cancelled. He cut the live calls from three a week to one, moved the big content release from monthly to quarterly, and turned off some app features. His rule: "you only introduce something when it's required or necessary for that person to get the the desired value." ([Less is More @ 11:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=695s))

**What would change his answer:** If your cancellation tags show price, not overwhelm, as the main reason, he'd change the pricing instead. That means a cheaper tier only if your ideal members are the ones saying it's too expensive, plus a discounted annual plan.

One caveat: this talk is built on data from Skool, a platform he promotes, though it matches what he says about running his own gyms.

**Verdict:** Keep the 9-to-5 for now and build the business in your mornings and evenings. Quit when two things are true: you have enough cash that rent is no longer a worry, and the job has started to feel like a cage. He doesn't think the job is what's holding you back. He thinks the hours around it are being wasted.

**Based on:** he said this directly about keeping the job and using the hours around it. When to make the leap follows from his principles; he never gives a quit trigger in so many words.

**Why he'd say it**
- The job isn't the problem: "Your nine-to-five job is not killing your dreams." What matters is "your five to nine in the morning and your five to nine at night." ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 3:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=194s))
- Cash comes first: "You can't think about your long-term vision if you're trying to pay rent" (@ 0:32). His order is to cut every cost, save, and avoid raising your lifestyle. In his words, "you get rewarded for the risk you take on. You cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money" (@ 13:04).
- He doesn't buy the idea that a job is the risky option: "as much as the entrepreneur talking heads want to say being an employee nowadays is riskier than owning a business. That's not really true." ([yt-rMJIOK_FgJk @ 1:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=66s)) But he adds that staying has its own risk: "the risk of not achieving what you want in life" (@ 8:49).
- What makes someone actually leave is the cage feeling: "if you don't feel like you're in a cage right now then maybe you're not in a cage and maybe you just need to like the life you have and that's cool too." ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 57:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=3470s))

**What he did:** At 22 he quit a consulting job he hated to open a gym, and it took him six months to go from deciding to doing it. He calls it "the hardest decision" of his life (@ 7:15). He says that if he had liked the job, he probably would never have left.

**What would change his answer:** If you hate the job and have little to lose, he'd lean toward going all in now. He sees "a capped downside, an uncapped upside" as "the recipe for opportunity" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 15:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=909s)).

**Verdict:** Offer a guarantee. He wouldn't make it a loose "refund if you're not happy" policy, though. He'd tie it to a condition, set the price high enough to cover the risk, and use it to make buyers believe they'll get the result. A strict no-refunds policy works against the variable he thinks matters most.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing from him on refund policy for coaching specifically.

**Why he'd say it**
- **It raises perceived likelihood of achievement.** This is one of the four parts of his value equation. In the ideal offer, the buyer would be "virtually guaranteed they would get it" ([video @ 1:22:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4928s)). A no-refunds policy moves that number the wrong way.
- **A guarantee is risk you can charge for.** "you can absolutely sell a guarantee" ([video @ 13:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=790s)). He also says "if something goes wrong, if something is delayed, if it if it's more difficult than expected. These are all things that you can choose to take on for a premium" (@ 14:15). So price the refund risk into the $2,000.
- **A higher price brings in fewer refund-prone buyers.** "you increase the emotional investment … and you decrease the demandingness of the customer" ([video @ 7:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s)).

**What he's done:** In a roofing consult, he suggested a priority fee that's waived if the deadline is missed: "if we don't we don't even charge it" ([video @ 18:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1113s)). That's a guarantee with a specific condition, not an open-ended refund.

**Not in the vault:** In *$100M Offers* he lays out a menu of guarantee types: unconditional, conditional (for example, refund if they did the work and didn't get the result), and an explicit "all sales final" stance. For $2,000 coaching, I'd expect him to pick the conditional one.

**What would change his answer:** a strong track record. "your reputation over time acts as almost an implied guarantee" ([video @ 14:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=885s)). With enough public results, the explicit guarantee matters less.

**Verdict:** Hormozi would tell you to wipe out the credit cards, get out of the car payment, and keep the rest as a cash cushion. He wouldn't tell you to put all $50k into the business. Any money you do put in should go to specific, cheap things that pay off, not a blind all-in bet.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing from him on personal credit cards or car loans. His view on business debt and his rules for personal savings settle it, though.

**Why he'd say it**
- He leans against debt: "I tend to skew like very close to the Ramsey side." His reason is that "Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 8:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s)). He backed a client's plan to pay off $60k of business debt within about five months.
- On cars, his answer is a downgrade, not just paying the loan: "ideally a paid-off clunker is the best way to go." ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 2:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=128s)). If the car is expensive, he'd likely say sell it rather than spend savings on it.
- He sees cash in the bank as what lets you take risks: "once I had $100,000, that was when I stopped having to worry about tomorrow" (@ 0:00). He also says "You cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money." (@ 13:04). Spending all $50k leaves you with no cushion.
- He still wants some of it spent on the business, in targeted places: "You've got tools, you've got implementation help, and then you've got trial attempts." (@ 11:25)

**What he's done:** He paid $400 a month in rent while his gym paid him about $20k a month, and saved the cash for a new location and for learning.

**What would change his answer:** if spending on the business already has proven returns, such as ads with a known payback. In one consulting session he called raising that kind of spend part of taking "greater and greater risk." He has never said when borrowing to grow is justified.

One caveat of my own: paying off credit cards at around 20%+ interest is a guaranteed return almost no business beats. On that point his view and plain math agree.

**Verdict:** For growing an audience, he'd tell you to start with short-form clips and post a lot of them. You learn faster from volume, and your winning clips can be reused as ads. Long-form comes later, to turn people who know you into people who trust you.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing where he compares long-form and short-form directly, so this comes from his principles about volume and content testing.

**Why he'd say it**
- He learns from volume: "you have to do a lot of volume in order to learn" ([video @ 9:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=588s)). Short clips give you dozens of tries a week, where long videos give you one.
- He tests content at scale: "every week we just blast off 30 videos up there and we see where the winners are." ([video @ 8:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=523s))
- Winning short posts also become ads: "when you find your winners, just take that same post, add a 5-second CTA at the end, and then run that as an ad." He calls this a "double dip" (same video @ [13:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=820s)).
- He treats a flop as useful: "You post this content, nothing happens. That is still feedback." ([video @ 9:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=588s))

**What he's done:** Acquisition.com gives everything away for free and aims "wide and deep". He says the free content brings companies to him before they've ever spoken to him ([video @ 2:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=172s)).

**What would change his answer** (not in the vault): his public advice elsewhere is that long-form builds depth and trust while short-form builds reach. His own setup is to record long and cut it into clips. So if you already have reach and need people to trust you enough to buy something expensive, he'd push you toward long-form. In either case, his "focus on one thing" principle says to pick one format and stick with it instead of half-doing both.

**Verdict:** Keep full price. If you want a Black Friday push, make the offer better rather than cheaper, and set a real deadline.

He thinks a higher price makes buyers more confident the course will work, and that a cut does the opposite. To him, a short window is a reason to act, not a reason to lower the price.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing from him on Black Friday or on discounting a course.

**Why he'd say it**
- Price raises perceived likelihood of success: "by raising the price, we actually increase the value." Higher prices also bring "emotional investment… the results" ([OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 7:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s)). A 30% cut works against all of that.
- Too few buyers means the offer needs work, not the price: "if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" ([x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:25:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5123s)). Not in the vault: his *$100M Offers* book argues for adding bonuses instead of discounting.
- A deadline is enough of a hook: "the key to making urgency and scarcity work is making it legitimate" ([JDR-R--4HhM @ 21:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=1310s)). So close the bonus window when you say you will. If you run a sale every November, people learn to wait for it, and "that's where you start losing power" (@ 23:05).
- Any reason for the promotion works, and "you get bonus points for a reason if you can tie it back to urgency or scarcity" ([JDR-R--4HhM @ 10:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=633s)). Black Friday is your reason. The discount isn't needed.

**What would change his answer:** He'd add a cheaper tier, not run a sale, if your *ideal* customers keep saying price is the problem. He ignores price complaints from people outside the target customer ([-j8_YCWZ05Q](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q)).

If you want to keep this answer, I can save it to `derived/` in the vault.

I couldn't find this in the vault. Searches for "sales manager", "promote", "best rep", "leader" and "manage" turned up nothing on promoting from within versus hiring from outside, and I also checked the raw transcripts. So the answer below is mostly my read of Hormozi, not something he's on record saying in these sources.

**Verdict:** Probably don't hand the job to your best rep just because they sell the most. Before you choose anyone, set up tracking for every rep. Then give the role to whoever can raise the numbers of the rest of the team. In my read (not in the vault), that's often a strong rep who wants to lead, not necessarily your top seller.

**Based on:** mostly beyond the vault

**What the vault does say**
- Once the owner stops being the whole sales team, tracking is the next thing to set up. In his roofing consult he says: "from a sales perspective, you're going to probably have to track this maybe a little bit more" and "as the team scales up, this is going to probably be the next piece that you're going to want to have to install" ([video @ 21:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1274s)). With per-rep numbers in hand, you can judge a manager by how much the team's results improve, not by your gut.
- He treats hiring salespeople like marketing to customers: "I want you to think about sales people as your new customers or your new avatar" ([video @ 21:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1305s)). If you need a pipeline of reps, recruiting probably becomes part of the manager's job, so test candidates on it.
- He screens for culture fit up front with values and concrete scenarios, like asking what someone does when a question comes in at 4:59 and their shift ends at 5 ([Diary of a CEO @ 1:16:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4568s)). Whoever you pick has to carry that culture.

**Beyond the vault:** I think he'd point out that your top closer brings in revenue directly. Moving them into management means losing their sales and betting on a skill they haven't shown yet. Being great at selling and being able to coach other people to sell are different abilities.

**What would change the answer:** I can't cite anything he's said on this. My guess is that if your best rep already coaches the others and their numbers go up, promoting them is the obvious move.

If you want the vault to answer this directly, it needs sources where he talks about building and managing sales teams. I can look for some and add them.

**Verdict:** Double down on the first business. Hormozi would say a $1M business has a lot of growth left in it, and a second line would take resources from the bet that's already working.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing where he answers "second business at $1M?" directly, but his views on focus settle it.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Pick one bet and stick with it.** "Sometimes you have to sit with the pain of an unbuilt bridge without building a second bridge." Trying several things at once "ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work but will take time" ([2025-05 @ 4:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=298s), [@ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s)).
- **Growth comes from saying no.** "the effort that it takes to compound is the length of time you have to say no to everything else" ([2025-11 @ 22:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1378s)).
- **The urge for a new business is usually a money-model problem.** "A lot of business owners think that they need to change something about their business or get into a different business" ([2025-08 @ 3:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=201s)). His fix is to "make more from each one" (@ 8:50).
- **Grow what you have before adding anything.** He splits growth into "get more customers, make them worth more." He'd squeeze the existing channel before opening a new one: "there's a lot more that you can work on the existing one by like a lot" ([2026-02 @ 5:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=327s)).

**What he's done:** He admits he usually breaks his own rule. He gets impatient after about 30 days and starts a second approach, and calls that a mistake. He did launch other companies (Prestige Labs supplements and ALAN software), but only after Gym Launch was making about $26M a year, and he sold them to the gym owners who were already his customers.

**What would change his answer:** a "second line" that is really an upsell or add-on to your current customers. That makes each customer worth more, so he'd count it as part of doubling down, not as a distraction.

**Verdict:** He'd probably tell you to keep it. At 3x profit, the business pays you the same money in about three years, and you still own it afterward. He'd sell only if you already know what you'd do next and have tested it.

**Based on:** follows from what he said, plus some things that aren't in the vault. The vault has nothing where he talks about a 3x offer directly.

**Why he'd say it**
- He starts by asking what you want, because that decides it. To an owner: "Do you want to double it? Do you want to sell the business? Or do you just want to make money with it?" ([yt-MH-IMJxbUY4 @ 4:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=263s))
- He counts owning the business as an advantage: "you keep the control and the equity… You decide the pace the strategy and ultimately you can exit on your own time horizon or never exit at all." The goal is "a compounding vehicle" ([yt-sL16tsGafcQ @ 3:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=225s))
- If you want a higher price, fix the business first. Making revenue recurring "is obviously significantly more valuable" ([yt-o64cI6tebnU @ 14:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=853s))
- **Not in the vault:** he often explains a profit multiple as payback. At 3x, the buyer gets their money back in three years. That price is low for a business that runs without you and typical for one that depends on you. Either way, he'd tell you to grow profit and get yourself out of the day-to-day before selling, so the multiple goes up.

**What he's done:** He sold two-thirds of Gym Launch and Prestige Labs in 2021 for $46.2M. He was willing to sell "because… the first three or four Investments we did did really well", and "I didn't want to be the gym guy for the rest of my life" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 32:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1972s)). Even then, he kept a third.

**What would change his answer:** If you're burned out on the business and already have a next thing that works, he'd sell, maybe keeping a piece the way he did.

**Verdict:** Probably neither. Hormozi would first ask whether the app removes your business's real bottleneck. If it does, he'd have you buy an existing tool before building anything. If it truly has to be custom, he'd have you hire a skilled developer, not learn to code yourself.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing on AI coding tools or on hiring developers specifically.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Find the bottleneck first.** For him, growing means getting more customers or making each one worth more. "we have to identify what the constraint of the of the system is" ([video @ 1:30:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5419s)). If the app doesn't fix that constraint, building it is a distraction.
- **Buy before you build.** On spending money when starting out: "the alternative is you could try rebuild the entire thing. Yeah, or you could just like go to grab a tool that's already there. Save yourself some time." ([video @ 11:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=717s)) He means off-the-shelf software such as a CRM or a landing-page builder.
- **Pay for skill rather than learn it slowly.** "The fastest way to learn skills is to find somebody who's really good and hire them one-on-one." ([video @ 9:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=588s)) He calls paid help "minor investments that will give you huge leverage on your time."
- **Protect your hours.** He splits his day into promoting, delivering and building the business's future: "if nobody knows about your stuff, they can't give you money" ([video @ 4:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=289s)). He also warns against starting side projects that "pull resources from the one way that I know will work" ([video @ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s)).

**What would change his answer:** if the software itself is what you sell, building it is your core skill, so you should learn it. (That's my inference, not something he said.)

**Where I'd push back:** AI coding tools have made a simple internal app very cheap to build. If it's a weekend project and your sales aren't suffering for it, building it yourself can fit his "minor investment" logic.
